nameStory: The Clymene moth gets its name from Clymene, a figure from Greek mythology who was one of the ocean nymphs called Oceanids. In some stories, she was the mother of Atlas and Prometheus, making her a fitting namesake for this beautiful moth. The scientific name Haploa clymene was first given to this species way back in 1776 by naturalist Peter Brown.
description: The Clymene moth is a striking member of the tiger moth family, known for its bold black and white patterned wings. These medium-sized moths have forewings that display dramatic contrasting stripes and spots, while their hindwings are often bright yellow or orange with black markings. Adults typically have a wingspan of about 1.5 to 2 inches across. Like other tiger moths, they're fuzzy and robust-looking, with thick, hairy bodies that give them an almost teddy bear-like appearance.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Forewings show bold black stripes and spots on a cream or white background, creating a striking zebra-like pattern that's hard to miss

idTips.label: Hindwings
idTips.description: Bright yellow or orange hindwings with black borders and spots, visible when wings are spread or during flight

idTips.label: Body Texture
idTips.description: Thick, fuzzy body covered in dense hairs that feel soft to the touch, typical of tiger moths

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized with a wingspan around 1.5-2 inches, noticeably larger than many common house moths

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Feathery or thread-like antennae that are darker colored and clearly visible against the pale head

habitat: Clymene moths are found throughout eastern North America's woodlands, forest edges, and suburban areas with plenty of native plants. They prefer areas with mixed deciduous and coniferous forests, especially where their caterpillar host plants like dogbane, milkweed, and various wildflowers grow. You'll often spot adults around outdoor lights in wooded neighborhoods, parks, and nature preserves from sea level up to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with the first individuals appearing in May as temperatures warm up consistently.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season runs through summer months, when adults are most active and commonly seen at lights. This is the best time to observe their striking wing patterns.
seasonality.fall: Flight activity continues into early fall, with some individuals still active in September before cooler weather ends their season.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not present during winter months, as they complete their life cycle and overwinter in other stages.

funFact: When threatened, Clymene moth caterpillars can actually 'play dead' by curling up into a tight ball and remaining motionless for several minutes, then suddenly springing back to life and crawling away when the danger passes - like tiny fuzzy escape artists!
confusionNotes: Clymene moths are most easily confused with other tiger moths that have black and white wing patterns, particularly the Leconte's haploa. Remember: Clymene moths have more distinct, zebra-like stripes on their forewings, while similar species tend to have more scattered or blotchy black markings.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'tiger moths,' these insects are actually more closely related to woolly bear caterpillars than to the large, tropical tiger moths many people picture. The 'tiger' name comes from their bold, striped patterns rather than their size or fierceness.
compareHints: While Clymene moths are the only Haploa species commonly found in New England, they're part of the larger tiger moth family. Compared to other tiger moths in the region, Clymene moths have particularly crisp, well-defined black and white stripes rather than the fuzzy or blotchy patterns seen in species like the Isabella tiger moth. Their bright yellow hindwings also help distinguish them from the more muted colors of many related species.
